extracted.intended_audience: Readers of The Spectator / general literate public (early 18th-century England)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, moral and social essays (issues of The Spectator) offering observations, anecdote, and prescriptive remarks about manners, fashion, art, country life, and writing. These pieces mix reportage, moral reflection, and advice for a general literate audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental mutual influence and consistent household culture
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Wife grows wise by the Discourses of the Husband, and the Husband good-humour'd by the Conversations of the Wife. ... Their Virtues are blended in their Children, and diffuse through the whole Family a perpetual Spirit of Benevolence, Complacency, and Satisfaction.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Parents' differing tastes and repeated interactions shape children's dispositions; mutual improvement between spouses produces blended virtues in offspring. Anti-pattern: Parents keeping radically opposed notions (one mocking theatre, the other reading romances) produces divided, disrespectful children (girls viewing father as clown; boys thinking mother no better).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeless portrayal in painting — avoid contemporary fashions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Great Masters in Painting never care for drawing People in the Fashion; as very well knowing that the Headdress, or Periwig, that now prevails ... will make a very odd Figure, and perhaps look monstrous in the Eyes of Posterity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: To achieve lasting dignity, represent subjects in enduring/idealized dress (e.g., Roman habit) rather than transient fashions. Example: painters dress illustrious persons in garments 'that never varies' so portraiture remains graceful to posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a single, constant dress instead of chasing fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: "I could wish ... that there was such a kind of everlasting Drapery ... and that they would agree upon such Fashions as should never be liable to Changes and Innovations. ... If instead of running after the Mode, they would continue fixed in one certain Habit, the Mode would some time or other overtake them, as a Clock that stands still is sure to point right once in twelve Hours."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/Advice: Country people ought to stop constantly imitating town fashions and instead keep a steady style; by remaining fixed they will sometimes be in fashion and avoid ridiculous oscillations. Example/anecdote: gentleman's practical advice—to plant oneself at a corner rather than chase a rambling fellow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and account for geographic lag in fashion diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations reporting that fashions reach different parts of the country at different speeds (e.g., "a Fashion makes its Progress much slower into Cumberland than into Cornwall," "the Steenkirk arrived but two Months ago at Newcastle"), and local variants of dress persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: When judging dress or behaviour in rural areas, allow for delayed adoption of metropolitan fashions; what is 'in' in London may be out or not yet arrived elsewhere. Examples: commodes, periwigs, muffs, and other dated fashions appearing at differing distances from London.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conserve local resources by not exhausting your own grounds (preserve game)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is usual for a Man who loves Country Sports to preserve the Game in his own Grounds, and divert himself upon those that belong to his Neighbour. ... By this Means the Breed about his House has time to encrease and multiply"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Practical rule for country-sportsmen: hunt away from one's immediate lands to allow local game to multiply and to make sport more agreeable when it is harder to obtain. Metaphorical application implied: spare what is nearest to you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good breeding measured by conduct toward strangers and humility of behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Ephraim's speech: "There is no ordinary Part of humane Life which expresseth so much a good Mind ... as his Behaviour upon meeting with Strangers ... Such a Man ... will not vaunt himself thereof; but will the rather hide his Superiority to them, that he may not be painful unto them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Good sense and true civility show in modesty, avoiding ostentation of knowledge or superiority, not taking advantage of captive company with improper talk, and rejoicing in peaceable demeanour rather than boasting. Example: reprimanding the impertinent soldier and preferring calm conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over appearance: fashions and dress are trifles compared to real worth
rubrics_metrics.description: "Modes and Apparel are but Trifles to the real Man, therefore do not think such a Man as thy self terrible for thy Garb, nor such a one as me contemptible for mine."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Moral admonition not to judge people by their outward dress; value character and abilities over apparel. Counterexample: locals astonished by London dress should not let appearance determine esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of effective periodical writing (what makes The Spectator valuable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimonial: "Each Paragraph is freight either with useful or delightful Notions, and I never fail of being highly diverted or improved. ... you make a deeper Impression, and affect the secret Springs of the Mind; you charm the Fancy, sooth the Passions, and insensibly lead the Reader to that Sweetness of Temper ... rouse Generosity ... inculcate Humanity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/Criteria for good essay: combine usefulness and delight; vary subjects; affect readers' imaginations and emotions delicately; blend entertainment with moral improvement; maintain accessible style that leads readers toward gentler temper and generosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiration for calm, generous, and heroic comportment at death as index of character
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is a sort of Delight, which is alternately mixed with Terror and Sorrow, in the Contemplation of Death. ... we are affected with these respective Manners of Behaviour, as we secretly believe the Part of the Dying Person imitable by our selves ... Innocent Men who have suffered as Criminals ... seem to be Persons of the highest Distinction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: The manner in which people meet death (resigned, cheerful, generous, heroic) is a standard of moral worth and provides examples to be imitated. Examples cited: Socrates, Phocion, Epaminondas; these dying conducts are praised as teaching virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence about itinerant groups (Gypsies) — expect theft and seduction risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative observations: gypsies are described as 'lawless vagrants' who 'steal People's Goods and spoil their Servants,' pick pockets, seduce servant-maids, and foretell fortunes while taking small sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Practical cautionary rule for country folk—be wary of gypsies: guard property and servants; do not be gullible about promises (e.g., fortune-telling often results in loss of small items); anecdotal examples of stolen poultry, picked pockets, and seductions.
